newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada seen poised for economic gains in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Canada seen poised for economic gains in 1997.

text.p: Canada's economy is expected to be one of the top performers among G7 industrialized countries in 1997, a Reuters poll of economists showed on Wednesday.
The quarterly survey, which polled 22 economists in Canada and the United States, predicted the Canadian economy would grow by 3.3 percent this year.
For 1996, Canada's gross domestic product (GDP) was seen growing by only 1.6 percent, according a similar Reuters poll of economists last October.
Low interest rates, a lower than expected federal budget deficit and improved consumer confidence were seen fueling Canada's rebound, said John Anania, an economist with Royal Bank of Canada.
"This growth is totally investment-led, with some pick up on the consumer side in 1997," Anania said. "Interest rates should stay pretty flat and that means continued above-trend growth."

Canada's central bank has cut its key bank rate by 500 basis points since May 1995 to 3.25 percent, allowing commercial banks' prime lending rates to fall to 4.75 percent, their lowest level since 1959.
Although Anania did not anticipate a major shift in interest rates, he saw some monetary tightening on the currency side.
The Canadian dollar is now worth about 74.48 U.S. cents.
Twenty of the survey's economists predicted the Canadian currency would appreciate to 77 U.S. cents by the fourth quarter of 1998.
A stronger dollar was seen posing a threat to Canada's growing merchandise trade surplus, which was expected to widen to C$7.0 billion ($5.2 billion) in the fourth quarter of 1996.
Canada posted a third-quarter trade surplus of C$5.4 billion ($4 billion) in the third quarter of last year.
Survey participants predicted Canada's quarterly surplus would rise to C$10.1 billion ($7.5 billion) by the third quarter of 1998.
Economists cited economic growth in the United States -- Canada's largest trading partner -- as the main factor in Canada's trade boom.
About 80 percent of Canada's exports go to the United States.
The one dark cloud in Canada's otherwise bright economic picture is the country's stubbornly high unemployment rate.
Canada's jobless rate was 9.7 in December. That was sharply higher than the 5.3 percent U.S. unemployment rate.
Economists predicted that Canada's strong growth and increased trade would shave only a small amount from the nation's jobless figure this year.
All survey respondents agreed that Canada's unemployment would decline gradually in the next two years. But only one economist forecast joblessness to fall below 9 percent this year.
